title: The A.I. apocalypse canon and why it matters
gist: Yglesias argues that A.I. catastrophic-risk worries should not be dismissed as 'science fiction.' Skeptics like Claire Lehmann and Steven Pinker focus on whether superintelligence is possible, but the real question is how it would behave if built. Fiction going back to Samuel Butler's 1872 'Erewhon' helps make that question clear. The preview cuts off early.

insights.claim: Yglesias argues that the crux of the A.I. safety debate is the consequences of superintelligence if built, not whether it is technically possible, and that skeptics like Claire Lehmann and Steven Pinker waste effort on the latter.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Moves the A.I. policy debate toward controlling capable systems, which supports safety-regulation momentum.
insights.quote: It’s one thing to debate whether something is or is not technically possible; it’s another to consider what impact it would have if it did occur.

insights.claim: Yglesias says he does not know whether Pinker or Dario Amodei is right about whether superintelligence is possible, a stance of agnosticism on A.I. capability timelines.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shows centrist commentators treating frontier-lab claims of superintelligence as credible enough to debate.
insights.quote: I have no idea whether Pinker or Dario Amodei is correct about the possibility of superintelligence
insights.locator: I have no idea whether Pinker

insights.claim: Recursive self-improvement has long been understood as dangerous, and superintelligent A.I. would be hard to control.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Core argument behind calls to regulate or slow frontier A.I. development.
insights.quote: We have always known that recursive self-improvement is dangerous.

insights.claim: Dismissing A.I. risk as 'science fiction' is a weak argument: the question has been considered by many non-fiction thinkers over 150 years, and fiction helps clarify what people disagree about.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Counters a common dismissal that has reduced political attention to A.I. safety.
insights.quote: The question of A.I. risk is one that has been considered repeatedly by a large number of people over the past 150 years, including by many who are not science-fiction authors.
insights.locator: Concerns about catastrophic risk from A.I.

insights.claim: Samuel Butler's 1872 'Erewhon' imagined a society banning machines after realizing they could evolve in a Darwinian way faster than humans because of shorter generation cycles and eventually displace humanity.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Fears of machine evolution displacing humans are old, which suggests this anxiety will keep coming back as capabilities grow.
insights.quote: machines could undergo the same Darwinian process as animals, becoming more and more advanced over time until eventually — due to the shorter generation cycle — they would overtake humanity

insights.claim: Frank Herbert's 'Dune' Butlerian Jihad, in which humanity gets rid of computers, pays homage to 'Erewhon', and George Eliot took Butler's Darwinian argument seriously in her 1879 'Impressions of Theophrastus Such'.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Cultural background for public attitudes toward bans on A.I.
insights.locator: The Butlerian Jihad in Frank Herbert’s
